passage: The email arrived at eleven at night, with the flat full of noise from Dilnaz's cousins rehearsing a song for the mehndi tomorrow. "We are moving ahead with other candidates," it said, in three polite lines. Zeenat read it four times, and each time it sounded as if the panel had looked at her and found her lacking. Her chest went tight. Dilnaz, her flatmate, dropped onto the bed beside her and read it too. "It's one hiring decision, yaar," she said, "not a report card on you." Zeenat had no time to sink: another application closed on Friday. She typed one polite line asking if the panel could share any feedback, stuck a note on her laptop that read "give numbers from the project", and opened the next form.

qa.q: When did the email arrive?
qa.a: The email arrived at eleven at night.

qa.q: What did the email make Zeenat feel about herself, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt hurt and judged, as if the panel found her lacking; she read it four times and her chest went tight.

qa.q: What would you advise Zeenat to do after sending the feedback request?
qa.a: Keep the note about giving numbers from the project and keep applying, since the application that closes on Friday is still open. 🙂

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see the email?
qa.a: Dilnaz sees it as one hiring decision, not a report card on Zeenat.

grounding: Zeenat takes a polite rejection personally but treats it as one decision: asks for feedback once, notes one fix and applies again.

passage:
Hey Anand,

You asked how the Pune job is going. It isn't. Three weeks ago the recruiter said on a call, "You are almost selected, just formalities." I told everyone at home. I stopped replying to two other companies, because why bother? Then nothing. I wrote once, politely, and again after a week. Still silence. I went from hopeful to confused to properly angry, and last night I wanted to send a nasty message. I didn't. This morning I reopened the mails from those two companies and apologised for the delay, and one has already given me a test date. I'm going to stop refreshing my inbox. If the recruiter ever writes back, fine.

Tarun

qa.q: How many times did Tarun write to the recruiter?
qa.a: Tarun wrote twice: once politely, and again after a week.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling by the end of the silence?
qa.a: Hopeful had turned to confused and then properly angry, to the point of wanting to send a nasty message.

qa.q: What did Tarun do that keeps other options open?
qa.a: Tarun reopened the mails from two other companies and apologised for the delay, and one has already given a test date.

qa.q: How might Anand read this email?
qa.a: Anand may feel for the frustration and be relieved that Tarun is choosing to move on instead of waiting.

grounding: A recruiter's 'almost selected' is followed by silence; Tarun follows up twice, keeps other applications alive and moves on.

passage:
Pooja texts her friend Vasudha from the corridor outside the interview room.

Pooja: My hands are like ice 😰
Pooja: What if they ask something I don't know and see I'm not good enough
Vasudha: Then say what you do know. Remember the broken dashboard story from your internship?
Pooja: yes. I have two stories ready. the dashboard one and the fee-collection project
Vasudha: And if you blank?
Pooja: "I don't know, but here's how I'd find out"
Vasudha: Exactly. Breathe slowly first.
Pooja: ok. they're calling me in

Two hours later.
Pooja: Done! Got stuck on one database question. Said I didn't know but told them how I'd find out. The panel nodded 🙂
Vasudha: So proud of you 🎉

qa.q: Which two stories did Pooja have ready?
qa.a: She had the dashboard one and the fee-collection project ready.

qa.q: What was Pooja afraid of before going in?
qa.a: She was afraid that if the panel asked something she didn't know, they would see she is not good enough.

qa.q: Why is saying "I don't know, but here's how I'd find out" a better choice than bluffing?
qa.a: It stays honest and shows how Pooja would work the answer out, while a bluff could fall apart on the next question.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel when Pooja reports back?
qa.a: Vasudha seems proud and relieved, replying "So proud of you" with a 🎉.

grounding: Before a panel Pooja fears being exposed, prepares real stories, breathes and says she does not know but how she would find out.

passage:
Subject: Congratulations (draft two)

Nazia,

Draft one is in my diary and starts "why her?" and that is where it is staying. This is draft two, and the part that matters is true too. When you called about the offer I screamed, and I meant it. You worked for that. It's the same company that turned me down last week, so my chest is a strange mix of warm and sour today, and I'm letting it be both.

Can you tell me how you prepared? Which case study did you use, and how did you answer the panel's question about failure? I want to learn what you did. Dinner is on me on Saturday 🎉

Shreya

qa.q: What did Shreya ask Nazia to share?
qa.a: Shreya asked how Nazia prepared, including which case study was used and how the panel's question about failure was answered.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Shreya have after the offer call?
qa.a: Shreya's chest felt warm and sour together, glad for Nazia and hurt about the company that had turned Shreya down.

qa.q: What did Shreya do with the envy, and why does that help?
qa.a: Shreya wrote the sour draft in a diary and sent an honest congratulation, so the envy did not turn into hoping Nazia would fail.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel reading this email?
qa.a: Nazia may feel warmed by the real congratulations and glad to share how the preparation went.

grounding: Shreya feels warmth and envy together when a friend gets the offer, keeps the envy private, congratulates honestly and asks how the friend prepared.

passage: Twelve minutes on the clock, eight candidates around one table, and a ceiling fan that drowned every third word. Kalyani's foot tapped under the table. Each time someone opened their mouth she heard a rival for the one seat, and she wanted to shout over the lot of them. She did it once, cutting off a boy mid-sentence, and saw the panellist's pen stop. Her ears went hot. Then Ritu, across the table, made a point about flexible hours that Kalyani had not thought of. Kalyani took a breath. "Building on Ritu's point," she said, "the cost side matters too," and she added two clear lines and stopped. The panellist's pen began to move again.

qa.q: How many minutes were on the clock?
qa.a: Twelve minutes were on the clock.

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel about the other candidates at first?
qa.a: She felt tense and competitive, hearing each of them as a rival for the one seat and wanting to shout over the lot of them.

qa.q: What could Kalyani try in the next group discussion?
qa.a: She could give clear points, credit a good idea from someone else, and leave space for others to speak.

qa.q: How might the panellist have seen Kalyani's two moments?
qa.a: Cutting a boy off may look like someone who struggles to work with others, while building on Ritu's point shows someone who can; the pen stopped and then moved again.

grounding: In a group discussion Kalyani sees others as obstacles and shouts one down, then credits a good point and contributes clearly.

passage:
Dinner, and Amma sighed before she even sat down.

Amma: The Menons' boy already has a job in Kochi. Joined last week.
Jomon: Good for him.
Amma: I'm only saying.
Jomon: You're only saying it every week. (He puts his fork down and breathes.) Amma, are you worried?
Amma: Of course I am. Papa retires in two years, and I lie awake thinking what you'll do.
Jomon: Then let me tell you properly. Three applications are in. Interviews on the 12th and the 20th. And I'm finishing the online course by month end. Give me till December, please.
Papa: Avni, let the boy eat.
Amma: December. I will hold you to it, mone.
Jomon: Deal. I'll tell you after each interview.

qa.q: When are Jomon's two interviews?
qa.a: They are on the 12th and the 20th.

qa.q: What is Amma worried about underneath the comparison?
qa.a: Amma is worried about what Jomon will do, since Papa retires in two years and she lies awake thinking about it.

qa.q: What could Jomon do to keep Amma reassured in the coming weeks?
qa.a: Jomon could tell Amma after each interview, keep his dates, and remind Amma of the plan he shared.

qa.q: How might Amma see her remark about the Menons' boy?
qa.a: Amma says she is only saying it, so she may see it as worry rather than an attack, though it lands as a comparison for Jomon.

grounding: A parent compares Jomon to the neighbour's son; Jomon hears the worry beneath, shares his plan with dates and asks for patience.

passage: I'm Madhav. The email said no, and I just sat on the stairwell outside the library with my laptop still open. Shankar found me there. He didn't say "it'll be fine". He sat one step below, ate half a samosa and passed me the other half. We said nothing for maybe ten minutes. Something in my chest let go, and I could breathe again. I had been telling myself I was one of the ones who fail and didn't deserve anyone's kindness. Then he said, "Walk with me to the canteen?" and I went. Next morning I sent the feedback request I had been avoiding. What I took from it is that comfort is not the same as fixing, and I needed the comfort first.

qa.q: Where did Shankar find Madhav?
qa.a: Shankar found Madhav on the stairwell outside the library.

qa.q: Why did Madhav feel undeserving of kindness?
qa.a: Madhav had been telling themself they were one of the ones who fail, so anyone's kindness felt undeserved.

qa.q: What small next step did Madhav take?
qa.a: The next morning Madhav sent the feedback request that had been avoided.

qa.q: What might have changed if Shankar had rushed to fix it?
qa.a: Madhav might have felt hurried or unheard, and the quiet half samosa and ten minutes of silence are what let the chest ease and breathing return.

grounding: A friend sits with Madhav after a rejection without rushing to fix it, Madhav accepts the kindness and takes one small step.

passage:
Subject: Thank you, and an update

Dear Shalini didi,

Thank you for Sunday's mock interview. I'll admit it stung when you said my answers rambled and that I kept looking at the table instead of at you. I went home a little red in the face, embarrassed at how much I needed to hear. But you were right. Since then I have cut my "tell me about yourself" to under a minute, practised with my phone recording, and written three project stories in a few lines each. The real interview is on Thursday and I will write to tell you how it goes. Thank you for giving up your evening for me 🙏

Lalremsiami

qa.q: When is the real interview?
qa.a: The real interview is on Thursday.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami feel about the feedback?
qa.a: Lalremsiami feels thankful but a little embarrassed, since it stung and left the face red but was needed.

qa.q: What does Lalremsiami plan to do after the interview?
qa.a: Lalremsiami will write to Shalini to tell how it goes, so the help is reported back on.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel on getting this email?
qa.a: Shalini may be pleased that the honest feedback was used and appreciated, and glad to hear how the interview goes.

grounding: A senior gave a mock interview and honest feedback; Lalremsiami thanks Shalini, applies it and promises to report back.

passage: I'm Alka. Bhupen and I were in the same batch, and lately his talk is all about how the process is rigged: referrals, polished English accents, seats that go by quota. I know some of it is true. Last month a panel asked where he learned his English, in a tone he did not like. But this week his laptop has stayed shut. Yesterday I mentioned two clerk openings and he said, "What's the point." Today, though, I found him in the library with a spoken English book, muttering the lines under his breath, and he sighed and said, "Unfair, yes. But I still need the job." Then he opened the form. I can't tell if he's bitter or planning. Maybe both.

qa.q: What did the panel ask Bhupen last month?
qa.a: The panel asked where he learned his English.

qa.q: What might Bhupen be feeling when he says "What's the point"?
qa.a: He may feel discouraged and bitter, though Alka can't tell for sure what is in his mind.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do with the parts of the process that really are unfair?
qa.a: He could name them honestly, then put effort into what he can control, like the spoken English practice and sending the applications.

qa.q: How does Alka see Bhupen's complaints?
qa.a: Alka accepts that some of it is true but worries the anger may stop his effort, and admits not being able to tell if he is bitter or planning.

grounding: Bhupen blames the system, which is partly true, and Alka watches him swing between shutting down and still applying.

passage:
Pantry, after the Monday review.

Pradeep: You okay?
Siddharth: Fine. (pause) My face is still burning. He read my report aloud in that voice and said, "Is this what they teach at your college?" Everyone laughed. He calls it directness.
Pradeep: I saw. That wasn't directness, that was mocking. The mistakes in the report you can fix. The way he said it is on him.
Siddharth: I froze. I couldn't say a word.
Pradeep: Most people do. Write it down today: the date, what he said, who was in the room. Every time.
Siddharth: For what?
Pradeep: For when you talk to HR, or to me again. And keep your CV fresh, quietly.
Siddharth: So it's not just me being oversensitive?
Pradeep: No. Find me on Wednesday and we'll go through it together.

qa.q: What does the boss call his mocking?
qa.a: He calls it directness.

qa.q: What was Siddharth worried about when asking whether it was just oversensitivity?
qa.a: Siddharth worried that the hurt might be an overreaction, which shows how much the mockery had shaken Siddharth's confidence.

qa.q: What steps did Pradeep suggest?
qa.a: Pradeep suggested writing down the date, the words and who was there each time, keeping the CV fresh quietly, and talking to HR or to Pradeep.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see the boss's behaviour?
qa.a: Pradeep sees it as mocking rather than directness, and says the way he said it is on the boss, not on Siddharth's report.

grounding: A boss mocks Siddharth in front of the team and calls it directness; a trusted senior helps see it as the boss's conduct and suggests notes, HR and exits.
